blocks.heading: Large Payloads Preserved as http_request Evidence

blocks.text: For web events across static, dynamic, and high‑interaction containers, POST requests with unusually large payloads are preserved as evidence with the http_request type. This applies to both Threat Intelligence (TI) decoys and internal decoys where the Services type is Web.
See image.
To learn more, see Viewing and Managing Evidence and Configuring Services on a Network Decoy.

The following ThreatParse rules that detect exploits of different application vulnerabilities were added:

table: Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution vulnerability in version 7.1.8 or earlier. The /auth/login endpoint issues anonymous JWT tokens without credentials, and the /runners/start endpoint accepts JavaScript payloads that run via Node.js child_process, allowing arbitrary command execution on the server.

Authenticated Remote Code Execution vulnerability in version 7.18 or earlier via the POST /runners/load-reader endpoint. The functionName parameter is directly interpolated into a JavaScript code template without sanitization. The require=null mitigation is bypassed via dynamic import().

Authentication Bypass vulnerability in version 0.4.41 due to a missing authentication middleware in Next.js API routes under /src/app/api/providers/. This allows remote attackers to enumerate, create, modify, or delete provider connections without authentication.

Reflected Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the workspace view of Dashy version 4.3.6 or earlier. The URL query parameter is passed directly to the src attribute in iframe without scheme validation, allowing an attacker to inject javascript: URIs that run arbitrary JavaScript in the context of the Dashy origin.

blocks.text: To learn more, see About ThreatParse Rules.

blocks.heading: Secuity Hardening for Landmine Agent Installation in macOS and Linux Endpoints

blocks.text: Security requirements were added for the /tmp/landmine.txt configuration file used during Landmine Agent installation on macOS and Linux endpoints. The configuration file must have the following requirements:

blocks.item: Be owned by root
Not be a symbolic link
Not be writable by non-root users

blocks.text: These requirements apply to Landmine Agents for macOS (Intel and Apple Silicon) and Linux (DEB and RPM) endpoints.
See image.
To learn more, see Installing a Landmine Agent on macOS and Installing a Landmine Agent on Linux.

blocks.heading: Support for Zero Trust Network Decoys with the Same Hostname

blocks.text: Support was added for deploying Zero Trust Network decoys with different FQDNs that share the same hostname. For example, decoy.corp-internal.com and decoy.corp.com, where decoy is the hostname, can be deployed as separate decoys without naming conflicts.
To learn more, see Creating a Zero Trust Network Decoy.

The following ThreatParse rules that detect exploits of different application vulnerabilities were added:

table: Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution vulnerability via the build_public_tmp endpoint in Langflow versions 1.9.0 and earlier. Attackers can submit a manipulated flow JSON containing Python code that is run during the build process without proper sandboxing.
Splunk Enterprise and Splunk Cloud Platform

Unauthenticated arbitrary file write/truncate vulnerability through PostgreSQL sidecar service endpoint due to lack of authentication controls. This affects Splunk Enterprise (versions 10.2.4 and 10.0.7 and earlier) and Splunk Cloud Platform (versions 10.4.2604.3 and 10.2.2510.14 and earlier). The vulnerability allows any network-reachable user to invoke file operations without credentials.

Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution vulnerability via PHP Code Injection in all versions of Everest Forms Pro plugin for WordPress up to and including 1.9.12. It allows unauthenticated attackers to inject and run arbitrary PHP code on the server by submitting a crafted value in any string-type form field (text, email, URL, select, radio) when a form uses the Complex Calculation feature.

Path Traversal Vulnerability in Langflow due to an unsanitized filename parameter in the POST /api/v2/files multi-part form data, which allows attackers to write files to arbitrary file system locations.

Unauthenticated SQL Injection vulnerability in the /api/v1/init_consts endpoint of Fortinet FortiClient EMS version 7.4.4 and earlier. The Site HTTP header value is passed directly into the PostgreSQL search_path without sanitization, which allows remote unauthenticated attackers to inject arbitrary SQL commands. This can lead to information disclosure, database manipulation, or OS command execution when chained with PostgreSQL functions.

Authentication Bypass vulnerability in Ivanti Endpoint Manager version 2024 SU5 and earlier due to improper access control, which allows remote unauthenticated attackers to leak stored credential data. The exploit requires no special privileges.
OS Command Injection vulnerability in Ivanti Sentry versions R10.5.2, R10.6.2, R10.7.1, and earlier which allows a remote unauthenticated user to achieve root-level remote code execution.

Authentication Bypass vulnerability in Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center due to an improper system process creation at boot, which allows unauthenticated remote attackers to run scripts and gain root access. The exploit requires crafted HTTP requests.

blocks.heading: Support for Data Collection Rule-Based Logs

blocks.text: Microsoft has deprecated the legacy method for receiving logs from SIEM platforms. To align with this change, Zscaler Deception supports modern data collection rule-based log ingestion for events and audit logs. This method requires predefined table schemas to define the expected log structure before ingestion.
If you are using Microsoft Sentinel SIEM configurations with legacy log ingestion methods, you must reconfigure them to use data collection rule-based log ingestion.
See image.
To learn more, see SIEM Configuration Guide for Microsoft Sentinel.

blocks.text: The following ThreatParse rules that detect different exploits were added:

table: DNS Active Directory SRV Record Reconnaissance

Detection of Active Directory (AD) SRV records from a decoy to locate domain controllers and directory services. Such reconnaissance queries are typically observed by AD enumeration tools like BloodHound or PowerView.
Detection of DNS ANY queries against a decoy. This method is used to rapidly map all record types in a zone.
DNSSEC Probe and NSEC Zone Walk Attempt

Detection of DNSKEY and NSEC records to perform a zone walk. This technique alphabetically enumerates all hostnames in a zone even when standard zone transfers are denied, indicating targeted reconnaissance.

Detection of NS records to identify authoritative name servers for potential poisoning or hijacking. Multiple internal zone queries suggest an attempt to map the full DNS infrastructure before an attack.
Detection of DNS NULL query, likely indicates the use of possible DNS tunneling tools like iodine for covert C2 communication. These queries bypass firewalls by encoding IP traffic within DNS labels.

Detection of PTR reverse lookups, which are used to map hostnames to IP addresses across a subnet. This passive sweep is commonly used early in reconnaissance to identify high-value targets like domain controllers.

Detection of SOA record queries, which are used to extract administrator emails and zone serial numbers for phishing or fingerprinting. This is a standard initial step for automated tools to identify primary name server targets.

Detection of a pattern of A, AAAA, and HTTPS queries for the same hostname confirms automated full-spectrum DNS enumeration. Tools like nmap or nuclei use these queries to map dual-stack network infrastructure.

Detection of DNS TXT queries that might indicate covert channel for data exfiltration, bypassing traditional security filters. High-entropy subdomain labels in these queries are commonly associated with malware implants.

Detection of WPAD hostname queries, which are often exploited by tools like Responder to steal NTLMv2 hashes. This might suggest a possible active attempt to redirect web proxy traffic to an attacker-controlled server.

Detection of DNS zone transfer requests (AXFR/IXFR) which are sent towards decoys to obtain a complete internal network map. This is a high-confidence reconnaissance indicator, as legitimate clients typically do not request transfers from decoys.

blocks.heading: Python-Based Handlers for Vulnerable Application Datasets

blocks.text: Python-based handlers are used to create and manage custom vulnerable application datasets (CVE datasets). Python-based handlers replace the earlier.the earlier YAML-based approach and this update enables more accurate and realistic simulation of modern vulnerabilities and attack scenarios.
This update provides:

blocks.item: Support for complex use cases, including multi-step exploit simulations (e.g., handling cookies and session flows).
Greater flexibility, allowing custom logic to be implemented using Python instead of relying on strict, regex-based YAML definitions.
Dynamic response handling, enabling handlers to generate runtime values such as random UUIDs and context-aware outputs.

blocks.text: To learn more, see About Vulnerable Application Datasets (CVE Datasets).

You can integrate Google Cloud Platform (GCP) with Zscaler Deception and deploy various GCP-specific resources as decoys. These decoys help detect malicious activities originating from adversaries within or outside your organization, depending on the type and configuration of the decoys. The following GCP-specific resources can be configured as decoys from the Zscaler Deception Admin Portal:

blocks.item: Service Account
Cloud Storage
Cloud SQL
Secret Manager
Artifact Registry

blocks.text: See image.
You can use Cloud Lures in landmine policies to deploy GCP service account decoys in endpoints to detect adversarial interactions with other GCP decoys.
To learn more, see About Cloud Deception with GCP.

You can deploy a generative AI (Gen AI) Model Context Protocol (MCP) server decoy that mimics a standard MCP server. The MCP server decoy integrates an AI application or a Large Language Model (LLM) chatbot with applications and decoy tools to generate fake responses.
See image.
To learn more, see Configuring Services on a Network Decoy and Supported MCP Server Decoy Applications and Tools.

RADIUS decoys that mimic real RADIUS servers can be deployed on your internal network via Internal decoys. These decoys respond to authentication attempts, lure the attackers, and divert any threat targeting your RADIUS network.
See image.
To learn more, see Understanding RADIUS Decoys and Deploying a RADIUS Decoy.

Cloud Deception provides Terraform support for deploying Zscaler Deception components and decoys in the Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Azure clouds. You can download a ready-to-use Terraform package that includes all configuration files required to provision the Deception resources and AWS and Azure decoys. This feature simplifies deployment at scale, improves reproducibility, and aligns cloud deception deployments with existing Infrastructure as Code (IaC) and CI/CD pipelines.
See image.
To learn more, see About Cloud Deception with AWS and About Cloud Deception with Azure.

blocks.heading: VPC Configuration Updates in AWS Cloud Deception

blocks.text: You can deploy RDS and VM image decoys in the Amazon Web Services (AWS) cloud by specifying the VPC or subnet information.
See image.
Deploying RDS and VM image decoys in the default VPC is no longer supported. Existing decoys that are deployed to the default VPC are not affected and continue to function as expected.
To learn more, see Creating an RDS Decoy in AWS and Creating a VM Image Decoy in AWS.
